keyTerms.definition: Whatever is in an effect must be present in some way — formally, virtually, or eminently — in its total cause, since a cause cannot give what it does not have.
keyTerms.example: You cannot get $20 from me unless I have the bill, the funds, or the power to produce the bill.

keyTerms.definition: The complete set of factors that together produce an effect — not just its material ingredients but agents, powers, and conditions.
keyTerms.example: A cake’s total cause includes the eggs and flour but also the baker, the mixing, and the oven’s heat.

keyTerms.definition: The cause has the very same kind of feature it produces in the effect.
keyTerms.example: Handing you a $20 bill from my wallet; a hot stove heating a pan.

keyTerms.definition: The cause has the effect’s content in a different mode — a power or resource that can yield it — rather than having the very feature itself.
keyTerms.example: Wiring $20 from my bank account so you can withdraw a bill I never held.

keyTerms.definition: The cause possesses something more fundamental than the effect’s feature, such as the power to make things of that kind.
keyTerms.example: Having access to the Federal Reserve press that prints $20 bills.

keyTerms.definition: “Action follows being”: a thing’s characteristic activities and attributes flow from and cannot exceed its nature, unless something else makes it act beyond it.
keyTerms.example: Plants grow and reproduce because they are alive; a stone cannot do these things on its own.

keyTerms.definition: An efficient cause brings about a thing’s existence or a change in it; a formal cause is a thing’s nature, what makes it the kind of thing it is. PPC governs the first; agere sequitur esse is its counterpart for the second.
keyTerms.example: The sculptor is the statue’s efficient cause; rational animality is a human’s formal cause.

keyTerms.definition: Applying a term to different things in exactly the same sense.
keyTerms.example: “Dog” in “Fido is a dog” and “Rover is a dog.”

keyTerms.definition: Applying a term to different things in completely different, unrelated senses.
keyTerms.example: “Bat” for the flying mammal and for the baseball club.

keyTerms.definition: Applying a term to different things in senses that are neither identical nor unrelated, because of a real relation or likeness between them. It is literal, not metaphorical (except in the metaphorical subtype).
keyTerms.example: “Good” said of wine and of a good man.

keyTerms.definition: A term applies intrinsically to one primary analogate and to secondary analogates only because of their relation (as cause, sign, or effect) to the primary one.
keyTerms.example: George is healthy (primary); food is healthy as a cause of his health; his complexion as a sign of it.

keyTerms.definition: A term applies intrinsically and formally to each analogate, though in proportionally different ways, grounded in a similarity of relations.
keyTerms.example: “Life” said of plants, animals, humans, and angels; “being” said of substances, attributes, creatures, and God.

keyTerms.definition: A term applies formally to one analogate but only figuratively to another, grounded in something intrinsic that resembles it.
keyTerms.example: “Lion” of the animal at the zoo vs. “George is a lion” because of his courage.

keyTerms.definition: A likeness of relations (A is to B as C is to D) that grounds applying one concept, indeterminately, to very different cases.
keyTerms.example: Eyes are to the tree as the intellect is to the Pythagorean theorem — both are “seeing.”

keyTerms.definition: A genus is a general kind; a specific difference is what marks off a species within it, and it lies outside the genus. Being is not a genus, because nothing outside being could differentiate it.
keyTerms.example: Human = animal (genus) + rational (difference); gold = metal + atomic number 79.

keyTerms.definition: Describing God by saying what he is not (immaterial, immutable). Feser holds it is part of the truth but cannot be the whole, since “God exists” and “God causes” are affirmative.
keyTerms.example: “God is not in time” is apophatic; “God causes the world to exist” is not.

keyTerms.definition: There is, and in principle could be, only one God, because a purely actual being cannot have the parts that multiplication within a kind requires.
keyTerms.example: Two humans differ by their matter; nothing could distinguish two purely actual beings.

keyTerms.definition: God has no parts of any kind — no matter/form, genus/difference, essence/existence, act/potency, or really distinct attributes. His real attributes are identical with each other and with him.
keyTerms.example: God’s power and his knowledge are, in reality, one and the same act of being, only analogous to power and knowledge in us.

keyTerms.definition: The mainstream tradition (Aristotle, Plotinus, Maimonides, Avicenna, Averroes, Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas, and others) for which divine simplicity is nonnegotiable and the core of the conception of God.
keyTerms.example: Taught by the Fourth Lateran and First Vatican Councils; affirmed by Luther and Calvin.

keyTerms.definition: The modern view (labels from Brian Davies and Norman Geisler) that treats God as the unique member of a species under the genus person, lacking our limits but not simple.
keyTerms.example: Plantinga, Swinburne, and Hartshorne are classified this way by Davies.

keyTerms.definition: Aquinas’ distinctions: the essence (what a thing is); a property in the strict sense (a feature flowing necessarily from the essence); a contingent accident (an intrinsic feature not flowing from the essence); a mere relation to something else.
keyTerms.example: Rational animality; the capacity to find things amusing; skin color; being Plato’s teacher.

keyTerms.definition: Wolterstorff’s term for the view, held by defenders of simplicity, that a thing’s essence and attributes are concrete constituents of the thing, not abstract Platonic entities it participates in.
keyTerms.example: Socrates’ rationality is part of Socrates, not a Form floating in a third realm.

keyTerms.definition: A change in what can be truly said of a thing that involves no real change in the thing itself, only in something related to it (Geach’s term).
keyTerms.example: Socrates becomes shorter than Plato when Plato grows; God becomes Creator when the world begins.

keyTerms.definition: Treating a feature that merely happens to accompany things of a kind as if it were essential to that kind.
keyTerms.example: Every professor so far has been under nine feet tall, so no professor could be taller.

keyTerms.definition: Immanent causation originates from within the agent (the mark of life); transient causation passes from one thing to another, as when a thing acts only because acted on.
keyTerms.example: An animal feeding vs. a thrown stone breaking a window.

keyTerms.definition: In Aristotelian metaphysics, the two principles composing every material substance: the form that makes it the kind of thing it is, and matter as the pure potentiality to take on form.
keyTerms.example: A dog is canine form actualizing matter; matter by itself is just potential.

keyTerms.definition: God’s mode of existence outside time altogether — not endless duration through all past and future time, but no succession at all.
keyTerms.example: Like an author conceiving a whole story in one flash rather than day by day.

keyTerms.definition: The view (Findlay; Russell against Copleston) that all necessity is a matter of linguistic convention, so a necessary being is nonsense.
keyTerms.example: “All bachelors are unmarried” is necessary only because of what “bachelor” means.

keyTerms.definition: A sentence is a linguistic item; a proposition is what it expresses, which can be expressed in many languages and would be true or false even if no language existed.
keyTerms.example: “Snow is white” and “Schnee ist weiss” express one proposition.

keyTerms.definition: Forming a mental picture versus strictly grasping something intellectually. Only imageable things can be pictured present or absent.
keyTerms.example: You can picture the numeral “4,” not the number four; nor can you picture God existing or not existing.

distinctions.name: Formal vs. virtual/eminent presence in a cause

left.label: Formal presence
left.desc: The cause has the very feature it produces — the heirloom picture: the $20 bill in my wallet that I hand over, the hot body warming a colder one.

right.label: Virtual or eminent presence
right.desc: The cause has the effect’s content as a power or a more fundamental reality: funds in the bank (virtually), control of the printing press (eminently). The effect’s feature may be a new, numerically different instance actualized from potency.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Almost every “counterexample” to PPC (sponge cakes, helium, a boy giving a black eye) assumes PPC requires formal presence. It doesn’t. And when we apply PPC to God, we mean that creatures’ perfections are in him eminently, not that God is literally spongy, material, or changeable.

distinctions.name: Univocal vs. equivocal vs. analogical

left.label: Univocal or equivocal
left.desc: Univocal: exactly the same sense (Fido and Rover are dogs) — applied to God it makes him a big creature. Equivocal: unrelated senses (the two bats) — applied to God it leaves our words empty.

right.label: Analogical
right.desc: Related but not identical senses, grounded in real relations or proportional likeness (good wine, good man; seeing a tree, seeing a theorem). Literal, yet flexible enough to span radically different kinds of reality.

distinctions.whyItMatters: This is how we can speak truly and positively about a God who is utterly unlike creatures, avoiding both anthropomorphism and agnosticism. It also dismantles Plantinga’s objection, which assumes God’s power and knowledge must be distinct because ours are.

distinctions.name: Analogy of attribution vs. analogy of proper proportionality

left.label: Attribution
left.desc: The perfection is intrinsic only to the primary analogate; secondary analogates get the name by relation to it (food and complexion called “healthy” because of George’s health).

right.label: Proper proportionality
right.desc: The perfection is intrinsic and formal in every analogate, though realized in proportionally different ways (life in plants, animals, humans, angels).

distinctions.whyItMatters: Both apply to God. By proper proportionality, being is really in God and in creatures, each in its own way. By attribution, God is the primary analogate of being and creatures are beings by relation to him as their cause. Attribution alone would risk saying God is “good” only in the sense that he causes goodness.

distinctions.name: Proper vs. metaphorical proportionality

left.label: Proper (nonmetaphorical)
left.desc: The form or nature is literally present in each analogate: plants and angels are both really alive.

right.label: Improper (metaphorical)
right.desc: The form is literally present in only one analogate and figuratively in the other: the zoo animal is a lion; brave George only “is a lion.”

distinctions.whyItMatters: Metaphor is a kind of analogy, but analogy is not all metaphor. When classical theists say God-talk is analogical, they are not saying it is poetry. Plantinga’s charge that analogy means “nonliteral” runs these together.

distinctions.name: Real change vs. Cambridge change

left.label: Real change / real property
left.desc: Something intrinsic to the thing itself is altered: Socrates grows hair; a person gains knowledge.

right.label: Cambridge change / Cambridge property
right.desc: What is true of the thing changes only because something else changed: Socrates becomes shorter than Plato because Plato grew; God becomes Creator because the world comes to be.

distinctions.whyItMatters: This single distinction answers Morris’s necessary/contingent-properties objection to simplicity and the “creating is changing” objection to immutability. God has contingent Cambridge properties, but no contingent real ones.

distinctions.name: Classical theism vs. theistic personalism

left.label: Classical theism
left.desc: God is absolutely simple: not an instance of any kind, not composed of attributes, the source of being rather than a being among beings. Personal in having intellect and will, analogically understood.

right.label: Theistic personalism (neo-theism)
right.desc: God is the unique member of the kind “person,” like us but without our limits; attributes are distinct; some (process theists) even allow change in God.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The difference is not personal vs. impersonal. It is whether God is the uncaused, necessarily unique First Cause or a supremely impressive creature-like being that could in principle have rivals and would need a cause. Only the classical God is what the five proofs conclude to.

distinctions.name: Everlasting duration vs. timeless eternity

left.label: Everlasting (longevity)
left.desc: Existing through all past time and all future time — endless succession, adding moments forever.

right.label: Timeless eternity
right.desc: Existing outside time entirely, with no before and after in one’s life; causing the whole temporal order in a single act.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Having no beginning or end is only the first step; immutability and simplicity push further to timelessness. Getting this right defuses objections that treat eternity as a moment (the Socrates–Obama simultaneity puzzle) or God’s causing as a series of acts.

distinctions.name: Imagining vs. conceiving (and possible worlds vs. essences)

left.label: Imagination-first modal method
left.desc: Picture scenarios (a lone green marble, then nothing) and read off what is possible or necessary from what we can picture or conceive in “possible worlds.”

right.label: Essence-first modal method
right.desc: Start from what actually exists, discover its nature, and infer what is possible or necessary for it — the Aristotelian-Thomistic procedure.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Schrader’s empty-world argument depends on the first. But neither numbers nor God can be pictured, and the second method is how the proofs establish God’s necessity. Picturing nothing tells us nothing about a being whose essence is existence.

illustrations.title: Three ways to give you $20
illustrations.body:
I can hand you a bill from my wallet (the effect is in me **formally**), wire money from my account so you can withdraw one (**virtually** — the total cause is me plus the account), or, if I somehow control a Federal Reserve printing press, have a genuine bill printed for you (**eminently** — I have something more basic than a bill: the power to make bills).

Use it to show that PPC never required the cause to *look like* the effect. God has creaturely perfections eminently, the way the press “has” $20 bills.

illustrations.title: The black eye and the hot iron
illustrations.body:
A boy does not need a black eye to give one to his neighbor (a Thomist writer’s point), and a hot body does not pass the very same heat it contains to what it warms. Instead, by its power it makes an actual new heat that was only potential in the heated thing (Aquinas).

The lesson: PPC is not an “heirloom” theory in which properties are passed down like jewelry. It says the effect cannot exceed the *powers* of its total cause.

illustrations.title: Seeing a tree, seeing a theorem
illustrations.body:
“I see the tree” and “I see that the Pythagorean theorem is true” use “see” in neither the same nor unrelated senses. The eyes are to the tree as the intellect is to the theorem — a similarity of *relations*. When we spell out each case (light hitting the retina; grasping logical relations among concepts), they aren’t two species of one genus.

So too with being: a man’s existence is to his essence as an angel’s is to its essence as God’s is to his — though in God, existence and essence are one.

illustrations.title: Zeus alone on Olympus
illustrations.body:
Imagine every Olympian god but Zeus vanished. Zeus would now be the *only* god — but his nature would be unchanged. He would still be the kind of thing there could be many of, a member of a pantheon with a single remaining member. The same is true of Odin alone in Asgard.

That is what denying divine simplicity does to God: even if in fact there is only one, he becomes one *instance* of a kind — unique by luck, not in principle — and a being that needs a cause. Feser’s verdict: a superangel, not God.

illustrations.title: Socrates gets shorter without shrinking
illustrations.body:
Socrates stays the same height while Plato grows; suddenly “Socrates is shorter than Plato” is true. Something new is true of Socrates, but nothing in Socrates changed — a Cambridge change.

When the world begins, “God is Creator” becomes true. The real change is entirely in the world coming to be. That is how an immutable God can have a contingent description without any contingent real feature.

illustrations.title: The nine-foot professor
illustrations.body:
Every college professor who has ever lived has been under nine feet tall. It would still be a fallacy to conclude that no *possible* professor could be taller: height is only accidentally connected to professorship.

Likewise, every agent we know changes when it acts (my fingers move as I type), and every living thing we know changes as it lives. But change is only accidentally connected to acting and living. What acting essentially is: bringing about an effect. What teaching essentially is: causing someone to learn — whether by lectures, books, or otherwise.

illustrations.title: The author and the whole story
illustrations.body:
An author might conceive an entire novel — beginning, middle, and end — in a single flash of insight. For the characters, chapter 10 comes after chapter 1. But the author did not think up chapter 1 first and chapter 10 later.

This is how God, outside time, causes a temporal world in one act in which things exist at t1, t2, t3. “God causes X to exist at t1” does not mean “at t1, God causes X.”

illustrations.title: Erasing “2 + 2 = 4”
illustrations.body:
Picture a universe containing only a chalkboard with “2 + 2 = 4” on it. Now picture it erased. Have you shown that 2 + 2 = 4 might have been false? Obviously not — you pictured numerals, not numbers, and numbers aren’t the sort of thing you can picture present or absent.

Schrader’s lone green marble works the same way: picturing it gone tells us nothing about God, who can no more be pictured than numbers can.

illustrations.title: Five roads to one summit
illustrations.body:
Five climbers ascend a mountain by five different faces — one by the scree of change, one by the ridge of composition, one by the glacier of abstract truths, one by the cliff of essence and existence, one by the path of sufficient reason. Each arrives at a summit that, on inspection, has the same features: no potency, no parts, existence itself, necessity. Since a mountain can only have one highest point with those features (unity), they are all standing in the same place.

A course analogy for the convergence argument; it also shows why the attributes are *mutually entailing* rather than a checklist.

illustrations.title: The light and the stained-glass window
illustrations.body:
Sunlight passing through a stained-glass window appears red here, blue there, gold elsewhere. The colors are really distinct in the glass, yet they are one light at the source. Our concepts of God’s power, knowledge, and goodness are like the colored panes: distinct in our minds because we meet those perfections separately in creatures, but corresponding to one undivided reality in God.

A course analogy for simplicity, with a caveat: God is not a physical light, and the analogy illustrates how distinct concepts can be true of one simple reality — it does not prove it.
